texts.preamble: Chiranji Lal vs Food Inspector on 4 March, 2021 The Court Of Shri Anil Antil Additional Sessions Judge-04, New Delhi District Patiala House Courts, New Delhi Criminal Appeal Number : 256/2017 Cc No. : 98/2011 U/S: : 16(1A) r/w Section 7 of P.F.A Act-1954 Chiranji Lal, s/o Sh. Budh Ram, Shop no. 9,Bijli Road,Pili Kothi, Naya Bazar, Delhi -6 .....Appellant versus Food Inspector, Department of Pfa, Govt of Nt of Delhi, A-20, Lawrence Road, Industrial Area, Delhi-110035 .....Respondent Appeal received by Predecessor Court on: 26.09.2017 And By this court on : 03.03.2020 Arguments concluded : 04.03.2021
texts.facts: 2. By way of present appeal, the appellant herein has CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 1 of 13 challenged the judgment dated 11.08.2017 and order on the point of sentence dated 24.08.2017 passed by the then learned ACMM-II, PHC, New Delhi vide which the appellant/accused was held guilty for commission of offences punishable under sections 16(1A) r/w Section 7 of PFA Act, 1954, the appellant was awarded a sentence to undergo Simple Imprisonment for one year as well as to pay fine of Rs. 50,000/- for commission of aforesaid offences and in dafault of payment of fine to undergo Simple Imprisonment of 15 days. Benefit of Section 428 Cr.P.C, if any, applicable was given to him. Chiranji Lal vs Food Inspector on 4 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168855141/ 1 3. The brief facts of the present case are that on 19.04.2011, the Food Inspector Sh. Ashok Kumar Singh and Sh. Pratap Raj, Field Assistant under the supervision of Local Health Authority/SDM Sh. R.K.Sharma, reached at the premises of appellant i.e. M/s Chiranji Lal Kiryana Store, Stall no.9, Bijli Road, Pili Kothi, Naya Bazar, Delhi where accused Chirangi Lal, Vendor cum Proprietor was found conducting business of various food articles including Dali Masoor Dal which were lying stored for sale for human consumption ; - that FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of commodity from the vendor which was lying in an open plastic bag bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed ; - that thereafter as per the prescribed procedure under the PFA Act and Rules after giving notice to the vendor/appellant and offer towards the sale price of sample to which he agreed and accepted the sale consideration, sample was then lifted ; CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 2 of 13 - that each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked, sealed and necessary documents including Notice as per Form-VI in the presence of appellant/accused alongwith Panchnama etc was prepared at the spot ; the price of the sample commodity was paid to the vendor ; - that thereafter one counterpart of sample was sent to Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA ; - that vide report dated 25.04.2011, PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it was coloured with synthetic colouring matter "Tartrazine & Orange II" ; - that upon receipt of report, SDM/LHA directed investigation which was carried out by Food Inspector and after completion of investigation sanction under Section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA. The complaint was then filed in the court on 25.05.2011 alleging violation of Section 2(ia)(a),(j) and (m) of PFA Act r/w Rules 23 & 29 of PFA Rules, as punishable under Section 7/16(1A) of PFA. Act. - that the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, hence, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with ; 4. The appellant/accused was summoned by the learned trial court vide order dated 25.05.2011 for 21.07.2011 to face trial. After filing appearance, accused filed an application under Section 13(2) of the PFA Act, thereby exercising right to get the second counterpart of the sample analyzed from the Central Food Laboratory (CFL). The application was allowed and the counter part CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 3 of 13 was sent to the CFL ; director CFL examined the sample and gave his report vide certificate dated 18.06.2011 opining the sample to be not confirming to the standards of Masoor Dal as per PFA Rules due to presence of non permitted colouring matter which Chiranji Lal vs Food Inspector on 4 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168855141/ 2 remained unidentified. 5. Thereafter matter was listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 Sh. A.K. Singh Food Inspector. 6. On the basis of testimony of prosecution witness (PW1) on 21.10.2013 charge was framed against the appellant/accused for commission of offences punishable u/s 7/16(1A) of PFA Act for violation of provisions of Sub clause 2(ia)(a)(j) and (m) of PFA Act alleging therein that on 19.04.2011 at about 09:00p.m. appellant/ accused being the Vendor cum Proprietor of M/s Chiranji Lal Kiyana Store, Stall no. 9 Bijli Road, Pili Kothi, Naya Bazar, Delhi was found present there and conducting business of various food articles including Dali Masoor Dal and sold for analysis 3 kgs "Dali Masoor Dal" ready for sale, taken from an open plastic bag bearing no label or declaration to Food Inspector on payment of sample commodity in the presence of LHA and witnesses and it was analyzed by the Director CFL vide Certificate no. CFL/331/353/2011 dated 18.06.2011 and opined that commodity is not confirming to the standards of split pulse (dal) Masur as per PFA Rules, 1955 because non permitted un identified colour was detected, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 6.1 During trial after the examination and detailed cross examination of three witnesses of the department i.e. PW-1 Sh. A.K. CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 4 of 13 Bhaskar, Food Inspector, PW-2 Sh. R.K.Sharma, District Officer, Social Welfare Department, District North-East, GNCT of Delhi the then Local Health Authority/SDM and PW-3 Sh. Pratap Raj, Field Assistant prosecution evidence was closed and matter was fixed for Statement of accused. 7. The statement of appellant/accused was recorded under section 313 Cr.PC in which he pleaded his innocence and stated that no efforts were made to join the public witnesses, payment was made, sample was not mixed properly, jhaba was not made clean before using it ; the relevant documents were not read over or explained to him before obtaining his signatures ; PA and CFL reports are wrong ; no adulteration was made by him, consenting authority has not applied his mind and dal masoor was purchased from M/s Parkash Traders Company, Naya Bazar, and he prefer to lead DE but no witness was examined despite opportunity. 10. During the course of argument on 04.03.2021, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that appellant is not challenging the merits of the case/ conviction decided by the learned trial court vide judgment dated 11.08.2017, and is confining his appeal limited to the quantum of sentence only awarded to him vide order dated 24.08.2017 ; and to affirm his submissions, appellant has tender his affidavit duly sworn and notarized by the Oath Commissioner, in that regard and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him by giving him the benefit of New Legislation as FSSAI. 11.
texts.arguments: II) Alternatively, on the quantum of sentence, relying upon the new legislation, it was pleaded that the case of the appellant be considered sympathetically in the light of the preposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Courts pursuant to coming of new legislation that is Food Safety & Standards Act. Learned counsel for the Delhi Admn./Food Department, objected to the same and submitted that according to submission of appellant, prosecution has established its case and he be sentenced with strict punishment in terms of old Act wherein minimum CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 6 of 13 punishment is prescribed and no leniency should be shown to the convict as it is a serious offence of food adulteration article / commodity leading to hazardous consequences on the health or body of a person. 12. 14. It is argued by learned counsel for the appellant that on the date of pronouncement of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed and new act has thereafter come into operation. It is stated that the court should give benefit of the new legislation to the accused vide which the punishment provided under the old act has been diluted to a considerable extent, and that the offence for which the accused/appellant has been convicted now falls under the category of "Unsafe Food" punishable under section 59(1) of the new Act i.e Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 7 of 13 FSSAI) punishable upto six months and fine of upto Rs. One lac only. Chiranji Lal vs Food Inspector on 4 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168855141/ 4 15. It was argued by learned counsel for the appellant that appellant is a man of 65 years of age, respectable person of society, has deep roots in the society ; was running small Kiryana shop for livelihood of his family, has left the business and settled in Rajasthan ; has responsibility towards his family, suffering from various ailments, not involved in any other similar case till date, and thus, prayed that a lenient view be taken against him in the light of the provisions of law under the new Act. 15.1 Further it is stated that case pertains to the year 2011, the appellant/accused has faced the trial almost 10 years which by itself is a sufficient punishment and, the hardships faced by him has caused him great mental agony, stress and rigors of trial during the said period. It is also stated that now a days special circumstances exists due to outbreak of pandemic of Covid-19 and there are chances of appellant being infected with virus in case imprisonment of sentence is awarded to him. 15.2 In support of his submissions qua the consideration of the case under new legislation, learned counsel for appellant had relied upon the judgment of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203 ) of Hon'ble Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai Vs. Henry 1983 ( ) SCC 177. 15.3 Per contra, learned SPP, strongly opposed the submissions CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 8 of 13 advanced by learned counsel by addressing that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences have changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged. Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed. Now FSSAI have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter" "unsafe food" and misbranded food". - Sub-clause (viii) of 3(zz) FSSA Act is applicable where the colouring material or the preservative other than that specified in respect there of is found in the food article and not where the colouring material exceeds the prescribed limit. Had it been the case, the charge would have been for the offence punishable u/s 16(1-A)(ii) of PFA Act r/w section 2(ia)(l) & (f). Chiranji Lal vs Food Inspector on 4 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168855141/ 5 15.7 15.8 Now, coming to the application of Nemi Chand Judgment (supra), the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T Barai ( Supra) of Hon'ble Supreme Court. The relevant portion of the T Barai Judgment is as follows : - (Para 25) It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication in Michell Vs. Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80 Lord Campbell put the matter thus : - "It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an ofence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute see also Smith Vs. Benabo ( 1937) 1 ALL ER 523 : ( 1997) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194" CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 10 of 13 - In Regina Vs. Youle ( 1861) 158 ER 311,315-16 : LT 299 : 9 WR 637 Martin B. said in the oft-quoted passage : - If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offence, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act." - The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different. - Moreover, this particular aspect is stated as a illustration in the same judgment in Para 23 which is as follows : - To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life, then it can not be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases. Chiranji Lal vs Food Inspector on 4 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168855141/ 6 15-A - Academic Reference can also be made to the letter dated 03.10.2017 of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, produced before the court during the proceedings. Vide said letter the said authority, in the light of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Nemi Chand's Case (supra) issued an advisory to the Commissioners of Food Safety/Officers incharge of Food Safety to CA no. 256/17 Chiranji Lal Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 11 of 13 dispose of the long pending court cases filed under old PFA Act mainly concerning substandard and misbranding by imposing fine only.
